But of course that's simply not the law. The coming and going exception holds that employers will generally not be held liable for the torts of their traveling employees and generally means that that rule is by no means absolute. So what is the standard for coming and going these days with regards to the doctrine of vicarious employer liability? Well, as the court is well aware, that standard was recently clarified by the Supreme Court in the Painter case or what I believe is commonly referred to now as Painter 1. And so to set the standard, the Supreme Court clarified that whether the employee was acting on a course in scope of his employment turns on whether the employee was performing the tasks generally assigned to him in furtherance of his employee's business. And the court goes on to say that there's sort of a two part component to that. There is the employee must be first acting within the employer's authority and secondly for the employer's benefit. And so the essential question as the Supreme Court in Painter put it was, was the employee undertaking a special mission on behalf of his employer or otherwise performing a service in furtherance of his employer's business with the express or implied approval as employer? In other words, was there some special benefit? This is also sometimes called the special mission exception but really special benefit is I think more appropriate for most of these cases.
